title: Raksha Bandhan
hook: a Hindu festival where sisters tie a thread on brothers' wrists, a bond of protection

segments.voice: Yesterday, Tu B'Av: the fifteenth of Av, and borrowed white dresses in the vineyards. Your line was dance in white. Who did you make room for? Today, another day of love, tied on with a thread. Day eight hundred seventy-six.

A plate on a small tray: a little lamp, a pinch of red powder, a few grains of rice, a sweet, and a bright thread with a flower of tinsel in the middle. A sister holds it. Her brother sits in front of her, wrist out, a little embarrassed, a little pleased. She marks his forehead, ties the thread, feeds him the sweet. He gives her a gift and a promise. In Hindu families in India and far beyond who keep the festival, scenes like this one fill a single day each year. Today: Raksha Bandhan.
screen: `A LAMP, A SWEET, A THREAD.` → `A WRIST HELD OUT.` → `A GIFT AND A PROMISE.`

segments.voice: First, the name. Raksha means protection, and bandhan means a tie, a bond. Put together, the bond of protection. The thread itself is usually called a rakhi. The sister ties it and prays for her brother's wellbeing, and the brother promises to stand by her. Second, the stories behind it. Hindus tell more than one. One, told in the Puranas, the old story collections, has the goddess Indrani tying a protective thread on the wrist of her husband Indra, king of the gods, before a battle. Another, a story people tell about the Mahabharata, has Draupadi tearing a strip from her sari to bind a cut on Krishna's finger, and Krishna, years later, protecting her in her hour of need. These are tradition's stories, told in more than one version, and people tell them for what they mean more than as history. Third, what the thread does. A rakhi is light. It snaps easily. It frays. Nobody is protected by its strength. The protection lives in what it stands for: someone remembered you, someone promised. The thread is the small visible end of a large invisible bond. Fourth, how wide it reaches. Some families tie rakhis between cousins, and between friends who have chosen to be like brother and sister. Some sisters tie them on sisters. Some people send them by mail across oceans when they can't be in the same room. The heart of the day isn't who ties it. It's the promise: I'm on your side, and I'm not going anywhere. Different traditions have their own days for love. This one ties love to a wrist, so it can be seen all day.
screen: `THE BOND OF PROTECTION.` · `INDRANI, DRAUPADI, KRISHNA.` · `A THREAD THAT SNAPS EASILY.` · `HOW WIDE IT REACHES.` · then, large: `RAKSHA BANDHAN.`

segments.voice: Rest your hands, palms up, on your knees. Feel the inside of your wrist, the place where a thread would go. Let the breath settle there. Now bring to mind someone who has stood by you, a sibling, a cousin, a friend, anyone who has been family to you. Remember a moment they kept you safe, even in a small way. Then, quietly, let them know in your mind that you're on their side, without conditions. Hold both of you in mind, as if one thread ran between your wrists. If you pray, you can ask for their protection in your own tradition's words. The bell holds the time.
Raksha Bandhan. The bond of protection, a Hindu festival when a sister ties a thread on her brother's wrist and he promises to stand by her. Today's word.
Your line: the thread. Today, tie a thread on someone's wrist if you can, or send a message to someone who's family to you that says simply, I'm on your side. Day eight hundred seventy-six.

howItsDone: On Raksha Bandhan, Hindu sisters tie a rakhi on their brothers' wrists, mark their foreheads and offer sweets, and brothers give gifts and promise their protection; some families also include cousins and close friends.

notes: A Hindu Keeper should confirm the Indrani/Indra story and its source (often cited as Bhavishya Purana, Uttara Parva); the script says only 'told in the Puranas'.
The Draupadi sari-strip story is not in the critical edition of the Mahabharata as such; the script calls it 'a story people tell about the Mahabharata'. Confirm framing.
Meanings of raksha (protection) and bandhan (tie, bond) are standard dictionary senses; confirm the Devanagari and pronunciation.
Hook mentions Hindu homes 'in India and around the world' and 'one day of the year'; no date (the Shravan full moon) is given, under the claims rule.
howItsDone says 'some families also include cousins and close friends'; soften to 'some' if the Keeper prefers.
Customs (tilak, sweets, gifts) vary by region and family; also kept in Jain and Sikh homes, which is left out to stay on the index's Hindu framing.
